## Multiple Logistic Regression

Just like linear regression, logistic regression also generalizes to multiple predictors:

$$
\log\bigg(\frac{\hat{y}}{1 - \hat{y}}\bigg) = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot x_1 + \hat{\beta}_2 \cdot x_2 + \ldots + \hat{\beta}_p \cdot x_p
$$

## Example: Diabetes and BMI {.t}

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=TRUE, size="footnotesize"}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
diabetes<-read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/diabetes.csv")
model_logit <- glm(Outcome ~ BMI, data=diabetes, family="binomial")
summary(model_logit)
```


## Example: Diabetes and BMI {.t}
Now we consider the full `diabetes` dataset:
```{r, echo=FALSE}
columns <- names(diabetes)[1:9]

description <- c("# of times pregnant",
          "Plasma glucose level",

knitr::kable(cbind(columns, description))
```

## Example: Diabetes and BMI {.t}

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=TRUE, size="footnotesize"}
model_logit <- glm(Outcome ~ ., data=diabetes, family="binomial")
summary(model_logit)
```


## Multiple Logistic Regression

Interpretation of coefficients:

- $e^{\beta_j}$ is the multiplicative change in odds of the outcome when $x_j$ increases by one unit and all other predictors remain constant

- Remember that $e^{\beta_j} \approx 1 + \beta_j$, if $\beta_j$ is small

\vspace{5mm}
Testing of coefficients:

- The reported p-value for $\beta_j$ tests the hypothesis
$$
H_0: \beta_j = 0 \qquad \text{vs} \qquad H_A: \beta_j \ne 0
$$
given that all the other predictors are included in the model.


## The Math Behind Logistic Regression

Error criterion for fitting:
\vspace{5mm}

::: {.t}
### Linear regression {.t}
\vspace{-2mm}
Recall that linear regression minimizes the \emph{mean squared error}:
$$
{\rm MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
$$
where
$$
\hat{y}_i = \beta_0 + x_{i1}\beta_1 + x_{i2}\beta_2 + \cdots + x_{ip}\beta_p
$$
:::

\vspace{5mm}
What is the objective function being minimized in logistic regression?


## The Math Behind Logistic Regression

Error criterion for fitting:
\vspace{5mm}

::: {.t}
### Logistic regression {.t}
\vspace{-2mm}
Logistic regression minimizes the \emph{log loss}:
$$
\text{Log-Loss} = - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left[y_i \log(\hat{y}_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{y}_i)\right]
$$
where
$$
\log\left(\frac{\hat{y}_i}{1-\hat{y}_i}\right) = \beta_0 + x_{i1}\beta_1 + x_{i2}\beta_2 + \cdots + x_{ip}\beta_p
$$
:::

\vspace{5mm}
Why?


## The Meaning of Log-Loss

Consider the loss for an individual observation $y_i$:
$$
-[y_i \log(\hat{y}_i) + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{y}_i)]
$$
Here are some possible values:

$y_i$ | $\hat{y}_i = 0.01$ | $\hat{y}_i = 0.5$ | $\hat{y}_i = 0.99$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
1 | $-\log(0.01) \approx 4.61$ | $-\log(0.5) \approx 0.69$ | $-\log(0.99) \approx 0.01$ |
0 | $-\log(0.99) \approx 0.01$ | $-\log(0.5) \approx 0.69$ | $-\log(0.01) \approx 4.61$ |

The log-loss represents the surprise of seeing the outcome given the estimated probability.


## Another Motivation: Maximum Likelihood

For those who took MATH 181A or DSC 140A, you may know that good estimators can be obtained by \emph{maximizing the likelihood function} of a statistical model.

- For linear regression, minimizing the MSE is exactly the same as maximizing the \emph{Gaussian} log-likelihood.

- For logistic regression, minimizing the log-loss is exactly the same as maximizing the \emph{binomial} log-likelihood.


## Binomial Maximum Likelihood

In logistic regression, the outcomes $y_i\in\{0,1\}$ are binary. Let $\hat{y}_i$ denote their corresponding probability. The probability mass function of $y_i$ can be written as:
$$
f(y_i) = \hat{y}_i^{y_i} (1-\hat{y}_i)^{1-y_i}, \qquad i = 1,\ldots,n
$$
Check: $f(0) = 1-\hat{y}_i$, $f(1) = \hat{y}_i$

If the observations are iid, then their joint probability mass function is:
$$
f(y_1,\ldots,y_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n \hat{y}_i^{y_i} (1-\hat{y}_i)^{1-y_i}
$$
Look at the expression as a function of the parameters. This is called the \emph{likelihood function}:
$$
L = \prod_{i=1}^n \hat{y}_i^{y_i} (1-\hat{y}_i)^{1-y_i}
$$

## Binomial Maximum Likelihood

The maximizer of the likelihood is the same as the maximizer of the log-likelihood:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell = \log L &= \sum_{i=1}^n \log\left[\hat{y}_i^{y_i} (1-\hat{y}_i)^{1-y_i}\right] \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \left[y_i \log(\hat{y}_i) + (1-y_i) \log(1-\hat{y}_i)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$
But maximizing this quantity is the same as minimizing its negative. Therefore, the maximizer of the log-likelihood is the same as the minimizer of
$$
-\sum_{i=1}^n \left[y_i \log(\hat{y}_i) + (1-y_i) \log(1-\hat{y}_i)\right]
$$
This is the log-loss! (except for a scaling factor $1/n$ that doesn't affect the minimization)


## Gaussian Maximum Likelihood

In linear regression, define the errors:
$$
\epsilon_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i, \qquad i = 1,\ldots,n
$$
If the errors are iid with common variance $\sigma^2$, then their joint probability density is:
$$
f(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\epsilon_i^2\right)
$$
Plug in the $\epsilon_i$'s and look at the expression as a function of the parameters. This is called the \emph{likelihood function}:
$$
L = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\right)
$$


## Gaussian Maximum Likelihood

The maximizer of the likelihood is the same as the maximizer of the log-likelihood:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell = \log L 
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \log\left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\right)\right] \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \left[-\log(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\right]
\end{aligned}
$$
But $\sigma$ is a constant, so it does not affect the maximization with respect to $\hat{y}_1,\ldots,\hat{y}_n$. Also, maximizing this quantity is the same as minimizing its negative. Therefore, the maximizer of the log-likelihood is the same as the minimizer of
$$
\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
$$
This is the residual sum of squares! (except for a scaling factor $1/n$ that doesn't affect the minimization)


## Conditions for Logistic Regression

 - The outcome variable is binary

\vspace{12mm}

 - The observations are independent of each other

\vspace{12mm}

 - The relationship between your covariates and the log-odds of the outcome variable is linear
 
 
## Conditions for Logistic Regression

 - The outcome variable is binary
   - This one is obvious

\vspace{10mm}

 - The observations are independent of each other
   - We could check residuals against time or something like that, but also can just make arguments based on anything we know about how the data were collected

\vspace{10mm}

 - The relationship between your covariates and the log-odds of the outcome variable is linear
   - We can check this one (somewhat) similar to how we checked for linearity in linear regression...


## Conditions for Logistic Regression {.t}
\framesubtitle{Linearity Condition}

Can we just check residuals vs. fitted values?

```{r, eval=FALSE}
diabetes$fitted <- model_logit$fitted.values
diabetes$residuals <- residuals(model_logit, type="deviance")
ggplot(data=diabetes, aes(x=fitted, y=residuals)) + 
  geom_point()
```

### What's up with the residuals(model_logit, type="deviance")?
\vspace{-2mm}
When using `glm` for logistic regression, it is customary to calculate "deviance residuals" instead of grabbing `residuals` from the model output. For our purposes, all you need to know is that they have better properties in a glm, and that you can get them with the above code.

## Conditions for Logistic Regression {.t}
\framesubtitle{Linearity Condition}
What exactly is happening here?

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%"}
diabetes$fitted <- model_logit$fitted.values
diabetes$residuals <- residuals(model_logit, type="deviance")
ggplot(data=diabetes, aes(x=fitted, y=residuals)) + 
  geom_point()
```

## Conditions for Logistic Regression {.t}
\framesubtitle{Let's illuminate this with simpler examples}

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, out.width="90%"}
set.seed(2)
x <- c(rnorm(30), rnorm(30, mean=2.5))
y <- c(rep(0, 30), rep(1, 30))

df <- data.frame(x=x, y=y)

ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method="glm", method.args=list(family="binomial"), se=FALSE)
```


## Conditions for Logistic Regression {.t}
\framesubtitle{Let's illuminate this with simpler examples}

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
model_simp <- glm(y ~ x, family="binomial")

df$fitted <- model_simp$fitted.values
df$residuals <- residuals(model_simp, type="deviance")
ggplot(data=df, aes(x=fitted, y=residuals)) + 
  geom_point() 
```

## Conditions for Logistic Regression {.t}
\framesubtitle{Let's illuminate this with simpler examples}

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
model_simp <- glm(y ~ x, family="binomial")

df$fitted <- model_simp$fitted.values
df$residuals <- residuals(model_simp, type="deviance")
ggplot(data=df, aes(x=fitted, y=residuals)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed")
```


## Conditions for Logistic Regression {.t}
\framesubtitle{Let's illuminate this with simpler examples}
So this is good, because the we are looking for the loess smoother to roughly follow the flat horizontal line at 0.

Here is the code that made the plot on the previous slide:
```{r, eval=FALSE}
model_simp <- glm(y ~ x, family="binomial")

df$fitted <- model_simp$fitted.values
df$residuals <- residuals(model_simp, type="deviance")
ggplot(data=df, aes(x=fitted, y=residuals)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed")
```




## Conditions for Logistic Regression {.t}
\framesubtitle{Let's illuminate this with simpler examples}

Now here's an example in which we have a questionable fit:


```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, out.width="90%"}
set.seed(2)
x <- sort(c(rnorm(20), rnorm(20, mean=3)))
y <- c(rep(0, 5), rep(1, 3), rep(0, 12), rep(1, 5), rep(0, 6), rep(1, 9))

df <- data.frame(x=x, y=y)

ggplot(data=df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method="glm", method.args=list(family="binomial"), se=FALSE)
```


## Conditions for Logistic Regression {.t}
\framesubtitle{Let's illuminate this with simpler examples}

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, out.width="85%"}
model_simp <- glm(y ~ x, family="binomial")

df$fitted <- model_simp$fitted.values
df$residuals <- residuals(model_simp, type="deviance")
ggplot(data=df, aes(x=fitted, y=residuals)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed")
```

This loess curve wobbles a lot, so this one is not so good.


## Conditions for Logistic Regression {.t}

## Spam filter {.t}

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=TRUE, size="footnotesize"}
#install.packages("openintro")
library(openintro)
data(email)
```

The \texttt{email} dataset in the \texttt{openintro} package contains 3,921 emails received by a single email account in the first few months of 2012, labeled for spam (spam: 0 or 1).


## Spam filter {.t}

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, echo=TRUE, size="scriptsize"}
model_logit <- glm(spam ~ ., data=email, family="binomial")
round(summary(model_logit)$coefficients, 4)
```


## Recap and Looking Ahead {.t}

::: {.t}
### Recap
\vspace{-2mm}
 - Logistic regression is used when we have a binary outcome variable, and any number of quantitative/categorical/binary covariates
 - $e^{\hat{\beta}_i}$ can be interpreted as an odds ratio
 - Logistic regression minimizes log-loss, not MSE
 - Conditions for logistic regression can be checked by looking at the residuals
:::
